reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: A slowly progressive form of autoimmune diabetes presenting in adulthood, often mistaken for type 2 diabetes at diagnosis
Distinguishing features include adult onset, the presence of islet autoantibodies (typically anti-GAD), and a lack of the marked obesity and insulin resistance often seen in type 2 diabetes
Unlike classic type 1 diabetes, beta-cell destruction is gradual, so patients may not need insulin for months to years after diagnosis
It sits on a spectrum between type 1 and type 2 diabetes and is sometimes called type 1.5 diabetes
Suspect it when a leaner adult with apparent type 2 diabetes shows early failure of oral agents or unexpectedly rapid progression to insulin dependence
Anti-GAD antibodies are the most commonly positive marker and support the diagnosis
There may be an association with other organ-specific autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease
Recognition matters because these patients progress to insulin requirement and benefit from monitoring beta-cell reserve rather than assuming a stable type 2 course
reference.pathophysiology: Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults is an autoimmune diabetes in which immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells proceeds more slowly than in classic childhood type 1 diabetes. Circulating islet autoantibodies, most often against glutamic acid decarboxylase, reflect this ongoing autoimmune process. Because residual beta-cell function persists at diagnosis, patients initially maintain some endogenous insulin secretion and may be controlled without insulin, but progressive loss of beta-cell mass leads to eventual insulin dependence. The disorder shares genetic and immunological features with type 1 diabetes while its adult onset and initial non-insulin-requiring course cause frequent misclassification as type 2 diabetes.
additionalInvestigations: Islet autoantibody testing, particularly anti-GAD antibodies
C-peptide to gauge residual beta-cell function and its decline over time
Screening for associated autoimmune disease such as thyroid dysfunction
Lipid profile and assessment of features of insulin resistance to help differentiate from type 2 diabetes
Periodic reassessment of beta-cell reserve to anticipate insulin requirement
redFlags: Development of ketosis or ketoacidosis indicating significant insulin deficiency
Rapid deterioration of glycaemic control on oral agents
Unexplained weight loss suggesting advancing insulin deficiency
Coexisting autoimmune disorders such as adrenal or thyroid disease
reference.prognosis: Patients generally progress to insulin dependence over months to years as beta-cell function declines; with timely recognition and appropriate transition to insulin, glycaemic control and complication risk can be managed similarly to other forms of diabetes, and monitoring for associated autoimmune conditions is advisable.
pitfalls: Assuming all adult-onset diabetes is type 2 and missing the autoimmune nature
Delaying insulin when oral agents are clearly failing
Not testing autoantibodies in a leaner adult with atypical type 2 diabetes
management: Transition to insulin replacement earlier than in type 2 diabetes as beta-cell function declines, since insulin dependence is ultimately inevitable
Avoid sulfonylureas, which may accelerate beta-cell exhaustion, and individualise use of metformin or incretin-based agents while endogenous secretion persists
Monitor glycaemic control with HbA1c and track residual beta-cell reserve with C-peptide to anticipate the need for insulin
Screen for and manage associated autoimmune disorders, particularly thyroid dysfunction
Provide structured diabetes education with dietary and lifestyle support and self-monitoring skills
Undertake systematic surveillance for retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and cardiovascular risk as in other forms of diabetes
Educate on sick-day rules and prevention of diabetic ketoacidosis, and refer to specialist endocrine and diabetes services
